title: Lattice–AMI U.S. government influence and regulatory-capture risk assessment
summary: Direct lobbying, federal-policy access, government product use, CFIUS protection, a trade-association revolving door and AMI participation in NIST rule-development are confirmed. Regulatory capture is not established.

data.question: What public evidence connects Lattice Semiconductor and AMI to U.S. government funding, procurement, standards and policy, and does it establish regulatory capture?
data.method: Primary-source federal lobbying, executive-branch, standards-comment and industry-association link analysis.
data.framework: Capture threshold requires evidence of preferential rulemaking, tailored procurement, suppressed competition, quid pro quo, or regulator dependence—not merely lawful lobbying or public comments.
data.scope: Lattice, AMI, federal lobbying firms, CFIUS, Commerce/NIST, Treasury and SIA records reviewed through 2026-07-27.
findings: Lattice paid Clark Street Associates $40,000 in 2024 Q4 and $40,000 in 2025 Q3 for lobbying that explicitly sought federal onshore-semiconductor funding and addressed Department of Defense appropriations.
The 2025 filing names the House, Senate and Department of Commerce as contacted institutions.
Clark Street publicly describes its semiconductor government-relations model as finding DOD and Commerce partners for development, demonstrations, sales and manufacturing scale-up.

House records expose a second lobbying layer: Holland & Knight registered for Clark Street on behalf of Lattice. An LDA lookup also lists FGS Global for Lattice, though the underlying activity was not resolved in this pass.
Treasury says the U.S. government uses Lattice products and treated Lattice supply-chain integrity as a national-security interest when CFIUS blocked a foreign takeover.
Lattice has direct executive access through SIA: then-CEO Jim Anderson attended a Treasury supply-chain meeting and current CEO Ford Tamer serves on SIA's board.
SIA's leader John Neuffer moved from senior USTR positions into semiconductor policy advocacy, while SIA publicly claims major manufacturing-incentive and federal-R&D policy victories.
AMI directly participated in NIST's CSF 2.0 public-comment process and recommended that software and firmware be included in Detect and Recover.

Coherent, connected through former Lattice executives and WEF membership, received a 2026 Commerce letter of intent for up to $50 million; this is adjacent evidence, not proof that Lattice or AMI received the funding.
Capture-risk indicator: recurring appropriations and industrial-policy lobbying
Capture-risk indicator: government customer and national-security protector
Capture-risk indicator: industry-board access to Commerce and Treasury
Capture-risk indicator: former senior trade official leading industry association
Capture-risk indicator: vendor comment on federal cybersecurity framework
Capture-risk indicator: parallel federal incentive awards in the adjacent Coherent network
conclusions: A durable influence architecture is confirmed: government customer/protector, recurring lobbying for public funding, multi-firm lobbying registrations, trade-association access and direct standards comments.
The strongest new regulatory link is AMI's documented attempt to shape NIST cybersecurity-framework treatment of firmware in a direction aligned with firmware-resilience products.
The public record reviewed does not yet cross the threshold from influence and structural dependency into demonstrated regulatory capture.
counterarguments: Public comments and lobbying are lawful, disclosed features of U.S. policymaking and do not themselves prove capture.
CFIUS intervention can be understood as national-security policy rather than preferential treatment.
SIA is a broad industry association; its wins cannot automatically be attributed to Lattice.
Coherent's CHIPS letter is not a benefit to Lattice or AMI.
limitations: The FGS Global activity, dates and issues were not resolved from the lookup record.
No comprehensive USAspending/FPDS vendor-identity reconciliation was completed for subsidiaries, resellers or product-level purchases.
Public-comment similarity to final NIST language cannot establish causation without NIST disposition records.
Lobbying reports disclose issues and contacts but not meeting contents or policy outcomes.
Capture evidence not established: Lattice- or AMI-authored language adopted into binding regulation
Capture evidence not established: direct federal award or procurement contract to Lattice or AMI
Capture evidence not established: procurement specification tailored to exclude competitors
Capture evidence not established: quid pro quo or campaign-finance exchange
Capture evidence not established: federal regulator moving directly into Lattice or AMI leadership
Capture evidence not established: causal proof that AMI's comment changed the final NIST framework
Capture evidence not established: WEF direction of U.S. policy or the AMI acquisition
unresolved: Exact federal contracts, grants or subcontracts involving Lattice or AMI products.
Federal Register comments and NIST comment-disposition records linking vendor proposals to final text.
CHIPS, DOD, CISA or NIST advisory committee participation by named Lattice or AMI personnel.
LD-203 political contributions by registered lobbyists and related PAC activity.
Whether procurement or cybersecurity requirements favor Lattice/AMI architectures over open or competing implementations.

caveats: Influence is confirmed; capture is not.

workflow.next_action: Test capture threshold through awards, procurement, advisory committees, rule text and contribution records.

title: Test Lattice–AMI federal regulatory-capture hypothesis
summary: Final-depth target to trace federal money, procurement specifications, advisory roles, rulemaking comments, political contributions and policy outcomes.

data.target: Lattice and AMI federal awards, procurement, rulemaking and capture test
data.research_question: Do public federal records show a preferential award, tailored procurement requirement, adopted vendor-authored rule, revolving-door appointment or quid pro quo that raises the Lattice–AMI network from influence to regulatory capture?
objectives: Reconcile Lattice, AMI, subsidiaries, former names and resellers in USAspending, FPDS and SAM.gov.
Enumerate all 2021–2026 LDA and LD-203 records for Lattice, Clark Street, Holland & Knight and FGS Global.
Search NIST, CISA, Commerce, DOD and Federal Register dockets for comments, disposition tables and named advisory participants.
Compare disclosed lobbying asks with enacted appropriations, grants, contracts and procurement language.
Identify any regulator-to-company or company-to-regulator personnel movement.
Record a bounded negative result if no evidence crosses the capture threshold.
selection_reason: Direct lobbying for federal funding is confirmed.
AMI submitted product-aligned comments to NIST.
Government use and CFIUS protection create structural dependency.
Capture remains unproven and requires transaction-level testing.

caveats: The target tests capture; it does not presume it.

workflow.next_action: Run federal awards, procurement, rulemaking and revolving-door verification.

title: Lattice–AMI U.S. government and capture-risk depth-4 pass
summary: Completed target shift from WEF representative mapping to U.S. federal influence, lobbying, standards input, government dependency and capture-threshold testing.

data.research_question: What U.S. government connections surround Lattice and AMI, and which are capture indicators versus ordinary disclosed participation?
data.method: Primary-source LDA, House, Treasury, White House, NIST, Commerce and SIA reconciliation.
classification_rules: Lobbying is influence evidence, not capture by itself.
Public comments establish attempted policy input, not adoption or causation.
Government funding to an adjacent organization is not attributed to Lattice or AMI.
Capture requires a preferential or exclusionary outcome linked to influence.

findings.finding: Lattice's direct federal lobbying for onshore semiconductor funding and defense appropriations is confirmed.
The U.S. government uses Lattice products and blocked a foreign takeover on national-security grounds.
SIA provides a current board-level policy channel and a documented USTR-to-industry revolving-door path.
AMI directly recommended product-aligned firmware resilience language to NIST.
Regulatory capture is not established at this depth.

provenance.method: Public-source recursive OSINT with bounded capture criteria
